meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The mind is like an iceberg, it floats with one-seventh of its bulk above water'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Freud. The “one-seventh” wording comes from physician Woods Hutchinson (1923); the simile itself dates to G. Stanley Hall, 1898.

answer.label: Not Sigmund Freud — a 1923 physician’s line
answer.authorDates: Hutchinson: American physician, fl. 1920s · Hall: 1846–1924, American psychologist
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Freud ever wrote or said this. Per Quote Investigator, the exact “one-seventh…above water” wording first appeared in physician Woods Hutchinson’s article in The Saturday Evening Post (March 17, 1923) — where the iceberg image was presented with no mention of Freud. The line was only pinned on Freud years later, in journalist William Leon Smyser’s 1929 New York Herald Tribune profile. The underlying iceberg-mind simile is older still, traced to psychologist G. Stanley Hall in 1898.

source.excerpt: The mind is like an iceberg which floats with only about one-seventh of its bulk above water and in the full light of day.
trail: Quote Investigator found the earliest version of the iceberg-mind simile in an 1898 article by psychologist G. Stanley Hall in the American Journal of Psychology, decades before the line was pinned to Freud.

The specific “one-seventh…above water” phrasing first appears in physician Woods Hutchinson’s article in The Saturday Evening Post (March 17, 1923), which presented the iceberg image without crediting Freud or anyone else. Freud’s name was attached only later, in journalist William Leon Smyser’s 1929 New York Herald Tribune profile “The Czar of Psychoanalysis” — the first source to credit the simile to Freud, and with no citation, per QI.
Wikiquote files the line in its “Misattributed” section, noting it was originated by others well before Freud received credit.
QI reports no substantive evidence that Freud himself ever crafted, wrote, or spoke this simile in any of his published works.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is documented to physician Woods Hutchinson’s article in The Saturday Evening Post, published March 17, 1923 — a U.S. work first published before 1931, and therefore in the public domain. author.name: G. Stanley Hall
author.kicker: The real source of the simile
author.heading: Where the iceberg simile actually came from
author.metaLine: 1846–1924 · American psychologist · first president of the American Psychological Association
author.bio: Granville Stanley Hall was a pioneering American psychologist and educator who founded the American Journal of Psychology and became the first president of the American Psychological Association. He is the earliest known writer to liken the mostly submerged mind to an iceberg, in an 1898 journal article — and, fittingly, it was Hall who brought Freud to America for his only U.S. visit in 1909.

misattribution.heading: Why this is pinned on Freud
misattribution.intro: The line fits Freud’s model of the unconscious so neatly that it became shorthand for it — but he never wrote it. The wording and the credit both come from outside his work.

items.why: The specific “one-seventh…above water” phrasing first appears in physician Woods Hutchinson’s article in The Saturday Evening Post (March 17, 1923), the earliest documented use of the one-seventh fraction — and Hutchinson gave the iceberg image with no mention of Freud, per Quote Investigator.

Freud’s name was attached only later: Smyser’s New York Herald Tribune profile “The Czar of Psychoanalysis” (1929) was the first source to credit the iceberg image to Freud, and it did so with no citation, per QI.

The earliest instance of this iceberg-mind simile known to Quote Investigator is Hall’s (1898), in the American Journal of Psychology — describing how most of the ego lies submerged like an iceberg; QI notes still-earlier iceberg comparisons but distinguishes them because they did not tie the hidden part to the unconscious, per QI.
QI found no substantive evidence Freud crafted the saying, and Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed.”

misattribution.truthLine: The iceberg image belongs to G. Stanley Hall (1898); the famous “one-seventh” wording belongs to physician Woods Hutchinson (1923) — not to Freud, whose name was only attached a decade later, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the myth sticks
lead: Freud did build his theory of mind on a hidden-versus-visible divide — the vast unconscious beneath a thin conscious surface — so an iceberg is an almost perfect illustration of his ideas. That fit is exactly why the metaphor migrated onto his name: it feels like something Freud would have said.

But feeling right is not the same as being sourced. The tidy “one-seventh above water” formulation was a physician’s 1923 phrasing — and Freud’s name was only attached to it later — while the iceberg comparison itself was already circulating in psychology a decade before Freud’s major works appeared.
detailsBody: Because it was never a fixed quotation, the fraction drifts from source to source — one-seventh, one-eighth, one-tenth above water (six-sevenths, seven-eighths, nine-tenths submerged), per Quote Investigator. A genuine quotation tends to have a stable wording; a floating paraphrase does not.
context.pull: The metaphor fits Freud so well that no one checked whether he actually said it.
